title: Telling a story
hook: Esther tells the king in Mordecai's name, and the name saves him; say where a story came from
tomorrow: who told the Buddha's own son to practice the breath?

segments.voice: Look at the week you just walked. Yunmen's every day is a good day. Seneca's evening court. Fatima's words for bedtime. The spice box at the end of rest. Yan Hui's narrow lane. And yesterday, Epictetus's sheep: show the wool. Now, the stories themselves, and how to hand one on.
screen: `A GOOD DAY · THE EVENING · GOODNIGHT` → `REST · PLAIN AND GOOD · SHOW THE WOOL`

segments.voice: A story is going around the group chat: a screenshot of a screenshot, and nobody knows who said it first. The book of Esther cares a great deal about who said it first. Mordecai, sitting at the king's gate, learns that two of the king's doorkeepers are plotting to kill him. He tells Esther, his cousin, who is now the queen. And she passes it on like this: "and Esther certified the king thereof in Mordecai's name." The plot fails. It's written down in the king's chronicles, and nobody thanks Mordecai. Then, one night, the king can't sleep.
screen: `A SCREENSHOT OF A SCREENSHOT.` → `MORDECAI HEARS A PLOT.` → `IN MORDECAI'S NAME.` → `THE KING CAN'T SLEEP.`

segments.voice: So he has the chronicles read to him, and there it is: Mordecai saved the king, and nothing was ever done for him. That sleepless night turns the whole story, at the very moment Mordecai's enemy Haman has come to ask for his death. Mordecai's name saved him, and it was there because Esther said where the warning came from. The rabbis built a teaching on that one line. Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, says whoever says a thing in the name of the one who said it brings redemption into the world, and it gives Esther as the proof. It's a living Jewish habit, and you can see it on the Talmud's pages, in chains like: this rabbi said, in the name of that rabbi. A story handed on with its source keeps its teller alive in it. So when you pass on a story from this path, Honi's carob tree or Yunmen's good day, the first line is part of the gift: this comes from the Talmud. This one's from a Zen collection.
screen: `THE CHRONICLES ARE READ.` · `THE NAME SAVES MORDECAI.` · `AVOT: IN THE NAME OF WHO SAID IT.` · `THE SOURCE IS PART OF THE GIFT.` · then, large: `SAY WHERE IT CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: Choose one story from this path you could tell in a minute: the carob planter, the sheep, the spice box. Tell it to yourself, quietly, out loud, and start with its home: in the Talmud, there's a man planting a tree. Then rest until the bell.
Telling a story: handing it on with its source, so the one who first told it travels with it.
The line for today: say where it came from, the way Esther spoke in Mordecai's name. That's the week.

chat.meaning: Esther told the king in Mordecai's name, and that name later saved him. Pirkei Avot teaches that saying who said it brings redemption.

Esther.meaning: the Jewish queen of the Persian king in the book of Esther

Mordecai.meaning: Esther's cousin, who raised her and sat at the king's gate

Haman.meaning: the king's official who plotted against Mordecai and the Jews

Pirkei Avot.meaning: the Ethics of the Fathers, a book of rabbinic sayings

Talmud.meaning: the collection of rabbinic teaching and debate at the heart of Jewish study

sources.quoted: and Esther certified the king thereof in Mordecai's name.

sources.ref: Esther 2:21-23; 6:1-4 (the plot, the chronicles, the sleepless night, 'there is nothing done for him', Haman arriving)
Pirkei Avot 6:6 (whoever says a thing in the name of the one who said it brings redemption into the world, citing Esther 2:22); also Talmud Megillah 15a
